title: This Simple File Management System Changed My Life!
summary:
• Good file management balances form (how neatly things are organized) with function (naming files so you can search for them quickly).
• Folder structure: at most 5 folder levels deep and up to 99 numbered folders per level; the most-used folders get the lowest numbers and 99 is always the Archive.
• His top level: 01 Personal, 02 Work, 03 documents he references regularly, 04 Quick Share (a temporary folder for copies made just for sharing), a Backups folder, and 99 Archive.
• Naming: time-based files get a year, quarter, month or full date (a year or quarter is the most searchable). Everything else is sorted alphabetically with consistent keywords like doc, meeting notes, briefing, slides, form.
• Five tips: organize by where you will use something (David Allen); use your file app's built-in search and filters; add keywords to file descriptions; star 5 files at most; add shortcuts to shared files. Don't over-optimize: pick one system and stick to it.

title: Google’s NEW Prompting Guide is Incredible!
summary:
• According to Google's prompting guide, the most successful prompts average 21 words, while most people type fewer than nine.
• Tip 1, the power of three: ask for three variations in your first prompt (slogans, ad copy, email templates) to surface options you wouldn't have considered.
• Tip 2, multi-step workflows: break a big task into mini milestones, each with its own prompt, instead of one huge prompt (what he calls chain-of-thought prompting).
• Tip 3: ask the AI to brainstorm templates for your role, then have it draft the most useful one. Tip 4: do top-down research, moving from a broad overview to specific, actionable prompts.
• Tip 5 (Google users): open a PDF from Drive in Google Docs and use Gemini's 'Help me write' on it (needs the Google One AI Premium plan). In his test, Gemini summarized several URLs better than ChatGPT.

title: Stanford CS229 I Machine Learning I Building Large Language Models (LLMs)
summary:
• Training an LLM depends on five things: architecture, training loss/algorithm, data, evaluation, and systems. The lecturer skips architecture and argues that data, evaluation and systems matter most in practice.
• Pretraining is autoregressive next-token prediction with cross-entropy loss. Tokenizers (e.g. Byte Pair Encoding) matter a lot, and models are evaluated with perplexity and benchmarks like HELM, the Hugging Face Open LLM leaderboard, and MMLU.
• Data means crawling the web (Common Crawl, ~250 billion pages, ~1 PB), extracting text, filtering harmful content and PII, deduplicating, filtering by rules and by model, and reweighting domains. Top models train on ~15 trillion tokens.
• Scaling laws: more compute, data and parameters lower the loss predictably, so you tune small models and extrapolate. Chinchilla found ~20 tokens per parameter (~150 if you count inference cost), and his rough estimate puts Llama 3 405B at ~$75M to train.
• Post-training turns an LLM into an assistant: SFT (needs surprisingly little data), then RLHF with PPO or the simpler DPO, with LLMs increasingly replacing human labelers and judges (ChatBotArena, AlpacaEval, which prefer long answers). Systems tricks include mixed precision and operator fusion (torch.compile).

title: Master Data Analysis with ChatGPT (in just 12 minutes)
summary:
• The three-step DIG framework (Description, Introspection, Goal setting), which he learned in a Coursera AI-for-data-analysis course, turns ChatGPT into a personal data analyst with no technical skills needed.
• Description: upload the dataset, have ChatGPT list every column with a sample value, take 5 more random samples, then run a data quality check for missing values, odd formats and outliers.
• Introspection: ask for 10 interesting questions the data could answer, which columns each one needs and whether the data is sufficient, and which questions can't be answered because data is missing.
• He joins a second (made-up) dataset on a shared ID column (IMDb ID), which unlocks new analyses like cost per viewer by genre.
• Goal setting: state your goal and ask which parts of the data to focus on, which gives you a step-by-step roadmap. Pro tip: before presenting, ask what questions readers of your analysis will ask.

title: Unlock Gemini’s Powers in Google AI Studio (Full Guide)
summary:
• Google AI Studio (aistudio.google.com) is a free, playground-style version of Gemini with more power and settings. It has four areas: Chat, Stream, Generate Media and Build.
• Its standout feature is video input: Gemini actually watches a video (or a YouTube link) frame by frame while listening to the audio. He uses it to reverse-engineer video prompts, analyze videos, and pull summaries and quotes from a pasted transcript to save tokens.
• Key chat settings: pick 2.5 Pro or Flash, a context window of a little over a million tokens, temperature as a creativity knob, media resolution (lower it only for very long videos), thinking mode, grounding with Google Search, a system prompt, and compare mode to test settings side by side.
• Stream lets you talk to Gemini by voice, show it your webcam, or share your screen. Screen sharing is good for help while working in a tool you already know the basics of, but he says it gets too much wrong to learn something from scratch.
• Generate Media makes images (Imagen 4), videos (Veo 2, four free videos a day), image edits and multi-speaker text-to-speech. Build creates working apps from plain-language prompts; he built a playable Pac-Man-style game in about four minutes. The catch with free: Google uses what you do there to train its systems.

title: How to digest 36 weekly podcasts without spending 36 hours listening | Tomasz Tunguz
summary:
• Tomasz Tunguz (founder of Theory Ventures) follows 36 podcasts but prefers reading, so he built a local 'podcast ripper' that downloads new episodes every day and transcribes them (first with OpenAI's open-source Whisper, now NVIDIA's Parakeet, which runs well on a Mac).
• Pipeline: download, convert with ffmpeg, transcribe, clean up the transcript with Gemma 3 via Ollama, track processed episodes in a local DuckDB database, then run a daily summarizer prompt.
• The daily summary lists host, guest, a comprehensive summary, key topics and themes, quotes (the most valuable part to him), investment theses for his VC firm, suggested tweets, and startups mentioned that could go into his CRM.
• Lesson: cleaning transcripts mattered when he used a Stanford named-entity library to find companies, but once he sent the text to a large LLM the cleanup stopped mattering much.
• A second workflow drafts blog posts in his style using his roughly 2,000 past posts as context (via a LanceDB vector database), then has an AI grade the draft 'like an AP English teacher' three times and iterates toward an A-minus. He says no model truly captures his voice, and he still posts by hand.

title: Give Me 9 Minutes, I'll Make You AI-Native
summary:
• Three levels of working with AI: AI curious (free tier, uses chatbots only when reminded or stuck), AI literate (pays for AI, keeps a prompts database, knows which feature and model to use) and AI native (has redesigned workflows assuming an AI collaborator exists). Most professionals are stuck at level two.
• Habit 1, leave AI breadcrumbs: copy the link to an AI conversation and paste it, with a note on why it matters, into the document where you use the output. Organize information by where you'll use it, not where you found it.
• Habit 2, build an AI swipe file: save excellent examples of work, then give them to the AI and ask it to analyze the key patterns in structure and tone and apply them to your new content.
• Habit 3, AI-first task planning: before a big project, break it into small tasks and mark which ones are manual and which use AI, and which tool (e.g. NotebookLM for fact-checking because of its low hallucination rate, the Gemini app for creative writing).
• Bonus habit: keep a prompts database organized by use case. He says you need 10 to 15 battle-tested prompts, not a thousand random ones.

title: Stop Learning n8n in 2026...Learn THIS Instead
summary:
• He argues AI automation is shifting from drag-and-drop builders (n8n, Make, Zapier) to agentic workflows built with tools like Claude Code, where you describe in plain language what you want and the agent writes, connects and debugs the code.
• He frames it as three waves: chatbots (ChatGPT), then AI plugged into automation platforms like n8n, then agentic tools that change how you build rather than what you build; each wave was a stepping stone, not a replacement.
• Side-by-side example: an n8n workflow that checks a YouTube channel every 8 hours needs a schedule trigger, HTTP requests, a database and deduplication logic you design yourself; Claude Code with Trigger.dev built the same thing from a description, including deduplication by video ID.
• Known pitfalls and fixes: context drift (shorter sessions, a project summary), hallucinations (always run and test what it builds, consider QA sub-agents), over- or under-engineering (be specific, use plan mode, let it ask questions) and production needs (error notifications, observability, version control).
• Live build: from one prompt, Claude Code created a ClickUp-triggered agent that researches a topic and posts a LinkedIn post plus a Nano Banana Pro infographic (via Kie.ai), fixed its own errors in testing, and finished a run in 2 minutes 23 seconds. n8n skills still matter as the foundation for directing agents.

title: The 5 Stages of AI Explained (Most People Don't Know What's Coming)
summary:
• The video lays out five stages of AI, saying we are around Stage 2 in early 2026: (1) large language models, (2) agents that perform tasks, (3) multi-agent teams, (4) artificial general intelligence (AGI), (5) superintelligence.
• Stage 1, LLMs like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok, predict the next word one at a time from patterns learned on huge amounts of text; he cites a Harvard finding that consultants using AI were about 25% faster with 40% higher quality. The ceiling: they tell you what to do instead of doing it.
• Stage 2, agents, act for you (Claude using a computer, Google's Project Mariner, Devin and Cursor for coding, Gemini scheduled actions), but they're still messy: only about a quarter of organizations have scaled agentic AI beyond testing.
• Stage 3 is teams of specialized agents (CrewAI crews, 'AI councils' that debate a decision, a bank's 12-agent fraud system); errors multiply at each handoff, companies underestimate costs by about 10x, and he expects mainstream adoption closer to 2030.
• Stage 4, AGI, is AI as capable as a human across any field (expert timelines range from 2026-27 to a median of 2047); Stage 5, superintelligence, could follow quickly through self-improvement. His advice: start learning early and build a system to stay current, shifting from doing raw work to managing and evaluating AI.

title: The only AutoResearch tutorial you’ll ever need
summary:
• AutoResearch is an open-source project by Andrej Karpathy where an AI agent runs experiments in a loop, keeps changes that improve a metric and throws away the rest; the core idea is one file, one metric, and hundreds of experiments while you sleep.
• It uses three files: program.md (the human's goal, constraints and rules), train.py (the only file the agent can change) and prepare.py (the evaluation, which the agent can never touch so it can't cheat). Each experiment gets the same fixed time budget so results are comparable; wins are committed to Git and losses are reset.
• It isn't just for machine learning: anything with a metric that's reasonably efficient to evaluate can be auto-researched, such as trading strategies (scored by Sharpe ratio), marketing tests, making code faster and tuning AI system prompts.
• Three conditions for success: one clear metric, automated evaluation with no human in the loop, and exactly one file the agent can change. It fails where 'better' is subjective (brand design, UX, most pricing), and a bad metric will be optimized very confidently.
• Demo: he cloned Karpathy's repo with Claude Code in Cursor, built a simple portfolio website, had Codex write a Puppeteer load-time benchmark, adapted program.md, committed a baseline, and let the loop run; median load time fell from 50 ms to 25 ms in about 4 minutes.

title: How AI agents & Claude skills work (Clearly Explained)
summary:
• Ross Mike's main point: the models (he names Opus 4.6 and GPT 5.4) are now very good, so what matters most is the context and the harness around them; less is more.
• Context is assembled from the system prompt, agent.md or CLAUDE.md files, skills, tools, the codebase and the conversation. He says 95% of people don't need an agent.md file, because it's added at every turn and wastes tokens; use it only for proprietary info needed in every conversation.
• Skills use progressive disclosure: only the name and description sit in context until the agent needs the rest (his example skill is 944 tokens in full versus 53 for name and description).
• Don't jump straight to writing or downloading skills. Walk the agent through the workflow step by step until you get a successful run, then have it review what it did and create the skill; when it later fails, fix the error with it and tell it to update the skill (he did five such loops on his report generator).
• Scale for productivity, not for what looks cool: start with one agent, build skills, then add sub agents when workflows are defined. Expect about 2 weeks of upfront investment, and keep the context window under roughly 70% full because models get worse as it fills.

title: Karpathy's LLM Wiki - Full Beginner Setup Guide
summary:
• The problem with RAG (retrieval augmented generation) in tools like ChatGPT or NotebookLM: every question searches your raw files from scratch, so nothing is saved, built up or compounded.
• Karpathy's LLM Wiki flips this: the AI reads each document once and integrates it into a persistent wiki of interlinked markdown files, updating pages, creating new concept pages, linking ideas and flagging contradictions.
• Three layers: raw sources (read-only, your source of truth), the wiki (markdown pages the AI creates and maintains) and the schema (a rules file such as CLAUDE.md telling the AI how to structure and maintain the wiki).
• Setup: install Obsidian (free, at obsidian.md) as the viewer, use a coding agent like Claude Code, create a vault with raw, wiki and optional templates folders, add a CLAUDE.md schema (change only the purpose line), drop sources into raw and tell the agent to ingest them; periodically ask it to 'lint the wiki' for contradictions, orphan pages and gaps.
• Limits: it works best at personal scale (around 100 articles), it's only as good as the sources you feed it, it needs a coding agent, and the AI can make mistakes, which is why linting exists; it's free and your data stays on your computer in plain text.

title: I Tested Gemini vs Claude vs ChatGPT So You Don't Have To
summary:
• He ran ChatGPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro side by side for 2 weeks with the same prompts across six rounds: writing, reasoning, coding, image generation, research and long documents.
• Writing went to Claude, whose output read like a person wrote it; ChatGPT was competent but flat and Gemini landed in the middle.
• Gemini won reasoning (he cites 77.1% vs Claude's 68.8% on a novel-problem benchmark), coding on larger codebases, image generation with Nano Banana 2 (Claude has no image generation at all), and research thanks to Google ecosystem and NotebookLM integration.
• All three now have a 1 million token context window; Claude had the most precise recall, but Gemini won the round because it can take video, audio, images, text and YouTube links in the same context.
• Verdict: no single model wins everything. Claude for writing and precise instruction-following, Gemini for large documents, reasoning and Google users, ChatGPT for the broadest feature set; for serious work use two and match the tool to the task.
